Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Print a values card per student, and keep the driving talk general: not everyone drives or has a car, and nobody shares what they’ve done.

Every student in the room

Family, faith, loyalty and community count as values at the wheel just as much as independence; say so when students pick five.

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

The brain vote, you are here, two speeds, pick five, and one if-then plan. Share the take-home for the rest.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Keep it light for ten seconds, then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

Hands up for each. Most will say 25; they’ve heard it. Then show the answer: “Good news, one part is done a lot sooner than you’ve been told.”

Slide 3 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 4 · Notes

Thinking it through (planning, reasoning, weighing pros and cons) is paved by about 16. The same in all 11 countries studied. Brakes under pressure (holding back when you’re excited, angry, or being watched) is still being built into your 20s. Point at the pin: “Great thinking, brakes still being built. That’s normal, not a flaw.” Say “into your mid-20s,” never “done at 25.”

Slide 5 · Notes

Tell a short, true story of your own: a plan you made calmly that fell apart with friends around. Keep it light and a little embarrassing, never dangerous or graphic. End on what you wish you’d decided ahead of time.

Slide 6 · Notes

Read the two bubbles out loud and let them laugh. “Same brain. On Tuesday the thinking lane drives. On Saturday, with friends watching and the clock ticking, the brakes get tested.” Hands only, no stories.

Slide 7 · Notes

Ask first: why do you think many states won’t let new drivers carry friends for the first months? Then: “Friends in the car turn up every teen’s reward system. Brain scans show it.”

Slide 8 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 9 · Notes

Two minutes in pairs. Talk about people your age, never about yourself or someone in the room.

Slide 10 · Notes

Take two or three. Say the realistic lines back to the room. Then two quick moments.

Slide 11 · Notes

With your partner: what would make it hard to say something, and what could you say? Not everyone drives; the passenger seat counts.

Slide 12 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 13 · Notes

Same two questions. A code word works best when the adult has agreed to it ahead of time. Some students won’t call police; a trusted adult or a friend’s parent is a full option.

Slide 14 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 15 · Notes

Teens gave more to a group when peers were watching (van Hoorn et al., 2016). “Your friends aren’t the problem. The volume on the reward system is turned up at your age. You choose what it rewards.”

Slide 16 · Notes

Read the labels out loud and take a few call-outs. Then: “All of those are real, and none of them is you. So what do you want steering instead?”

Slide 17 · Notes

Olympic final, teammates counting on her, millions watching. She had the “twisties,” losing track of herself in the air. She steered by what she valued: her safety, her health, her team’s best lineup. Ask: “What did she have to know about herself first?”

Slide 18 · Notes

Say it with a smile: “So no rules today. We’re going to ask what you care about.”

Slide 19 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 20 · Notes

Hand out the values cards. Two quiet minutes. Say out loud: family, faith, loyalty and community are values at the wheel, not someone else driving.

Slide 21 · Notes

One minute each, then hear a few lines. Celebrate funny, realistic ones.

Slide 22 · Notes

Take a few. Then three quick moments, one at a time.

Slide 23 · Notes

What would your star value do, and what’s the exact line?

Slide 24 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 25 · Notes

Same question. Hear a few lines.

Slide 26 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 27 · Notes

Point out that blaming a parent, a game tomorrow or a curfew are all real moves.

Slide 28 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 29 · Notes

If-then plans work because the hot moment only has to remember one line. Across 94 studies, people with if-then plans followed through much more often (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006). Set up a code word with an adult tonight.

Slide 30 · Notes

Two quiet minutes. Suggest a wallet, a phone case or a visor. “You made that plan in a calm moment. That’s the version of you who should be driving.”

Slide 31 · Notes

A license costs money; use the car as a picture of who decides. ADHD changes how the brakes feel, so avoid “just think first.” Some students fear police contact; a code word or a trusted adult’s pickup is a full option.

Slide 32 · Notes

Two minutes in pairs. Nobody speaks for a group, and no personal stories.

Slide 33 · Notes

Take a few. Listen for strengths as well as costs: family, faith, a friend who has your back.

Slide 34 · Notes

Share the take-home link. Ask students to keep their values card; later lessons use it. If a student mentions riding with an impaired driver or anything worse, thank them and follow up one on one that day.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can say where a 16-year-old brain is (adult-level reasoning when things are calm, brakes for heated moments still being built), explain why friends watching changes teen choices, name the five values they want steering, and write one if-then plan made in a calm moment for a heated one. Nobody is asked what they've done.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • A values card for every student: 24 values on the front, “If ___, then I’ll ___” on the back (the list is in the notes for the Pick five slide)
  • Pens or pencils
  • The take-home link to share afterward

Flow

  1. 2 minQuick vote: when is a brain done?
  2. 7 minYou are here, and your own true story
  3. 5 minTwo speeds, and the driving game
  4. 6 minTurn and talk, share out, then two moments: the ride home and 11:14
  5. 5 minGood risks, and who’s grabbing the wheel
  6. 5 minA real story (Simone Biles) and the research guess
  7. 4 minPick five
  8. 7 minYour star value: turn and talk, then three moments
  9. 4 minDecide cold, write your plan, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

The brain vote, you are here, two speeds, pick five, and one if-then plan. Share the take-home for the rest.

Before you teach
Skip "your brain is broken."

Teens hear "your brain isn't done until 25" as an insult or an excuse. The research gives better news: when it's calm, a 16-year-old reasons as well as an adult. Keep coming back to that.

The 25 number is softer than it sounds.

It comes from scan studies where change slowed in the mid-20s. Brains keep changing for life. Say "into your mid-20s," not "done at 25."

Keep it in the car on the slide.

The car at 11:14 is made up. Don't ask who has been in that car or what happened there.

Not everyone drives.

Some students won't get a license this year for money, family or other reasons. The passenger seat counts. The driver's seat in this talk means who decides.

Big room, small moves.

In a grade meeting, keep participation low-risk: hands, cards, standing up. Nobody talks into a microphone about themselves.

If someone tells you something.

If a student mentions riding with an impaired driver, or anything worse, thank them and follow up one on one that day.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Values aren't only individual.

Many students come from families and cultures where duty, family honor, faith and community come first. Those are values at the wheel, not someone else driving.

Independence means different things.

The research framed healthy choices as not being manipulated by people selling you something. That's different from going against your family. Say so out loud.

A license costs money.

Driver's ed, a car and insurance aren't equally available. Use the car as a picture of who decides, and never as a status marker.

Police and the 911 call.

Some students fear what police contact could mean for them or their family. A code word, a trusted adult's pickup, or a friend's parent are full options, not the backup plan.

Brains differ.

ADHD and other differences change how the brakes feel. Impulsivity isn't a character flaw. Avoid "just think first."

Every gender, every friend group.

Pressure isn't only boys daring boys. It shows up in group chats, on teams, in quiet friend groups. Use varied names and examples.

What the research says

Across 5,227 people ages 10 to 30 in 11 countries, reasoning and planning (cognitive capacity) leveled off at adult levels around 16. The ability to hold back when excited or pressured (psychosocial maturity) kept developing past 18 and into the 20s. The authors call the difference a "maturity gap."

Icenogle et al., Law and Human Behavior, 2019

Teens, college students and adults played a driving game alone or with two friends watching. Alone, the groups drove much the same. With friends watching, teens took more risks, college students somewhat more, and adults no more than alone.

Gardner & Steinberg, Developmental Psychology, 2005

In brain scans during the same kind of driving game, reward regions were more active in teens when they knew friends were watching. Adults showed no such change.

Chein, Albert, O'Brien, Uckert & Steinberg, Developmental Science, 2011

Peers push the other way too: 12- to 16-year-olds gave more to a group in a public goods game when same-age peers were watching, and more again when peers approved of giving.

van Hoorn et al., Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, 2016

In a randomized study of 536 eighth graders, standard health lessons did little. A lesson exposing how food marketers try to manipulate teens, framed around independence and fairness, led students to choose fewer sugary snacks and drinks. A follow-up found boys cut junk-food purchases by about a third for the rest of the semester.

Bryan, Yeager et al., PNAS, 2016; Bryan et al., Nature Human Behaviour, 2019

Across 94 studies, people who made if-then plans ("If X happens, I'll do Y") followed through on goals much more often than people who only set the goal.

Gollwitzer & Sheeran, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 2006

At the Tokyo Olympics (held in 2021), Simone Biles withdrew from the women's team final after one vault, citing the "twisties" and her mental health, and later withdrew from other finals. She returned to win bronze on the balance beam.

Widely reported, July and August 2021

In Massachusetts, a junior operator can't drive with passengers under 18 (other than immediate family) for the first six months, or drive between 12:30 and 5 a.m. without a parent.

Massachusetts General Laws c.90 §8; mass.gov Teen Drivers
